title: Cosmochemistry and Earth's Bulk Composition
description: From the solar nebula to a differentiated planet

concepts.title: CI Chondrites as the Solar Yardstick
concepts.contentHtml:
The composition of the Sun (excluding H, He, and other volatiles) and the composition of the most primitive meteorites — the CI carbonaceous chondrites like Orgueil and Ivuna — agree to within roughly a factor of two for nearly all elements. CI chondrites never melted, never differentiated, and have escaped major thermal processing since 4.567 Ga. They are our closest available sample of average solar-system non-volatile matter.

Geochemists therefore normalise rock compositions to CI to look for enrichments and depletions. Plotting Element/CI ratio against atomic number on a log scale immediately reveals the volatile depletion of Earth, the iron enrichment of the core, and the depletion of moderately siderophile elements in the silicate mantle from core formation.

The reference Allende meteorite (CV3) gave the first robust Pb-Pb isochron yielding 4.566 ± 0.002 Ga, a number that anchors the entire solar-system chronology. CI is the yardstick; Allende is the clock.

concepts.title: The Condensation Sequence
concepts.contentHtml:
As a hot solar nebula cools at roughly 10⁻⁴ bar total pressure, equilibrium thermodynamics predicts a specific order in which solids precipitate from the gas. Refractory oxides such as corundum (Al₂O₃) and perovskite (CaTiO₃) condense first at ~1700 K, followed by Ca-Al-rich silicates (melilite, hibonite) — the same minerals seen in the white CAIs (calcium-aluminium-rich inclusions) of Allende. Forsteritic olivine and metallic Fe-Ni follow near 1450 K; the dominant Mg-silicates (enstatite) and FeS (troilite) appear at lower temperatures.

Below ~700 K, hydrated phyllosilicates and the most volatile elements (Pb, Bi, Tl, In) finally condense, but only in CI- and CM-class chondrites that formed far from the Sun. Earth, having accreted closer to the Sun, is missing roughly 90% of its CI complement of these volatile elements.

The 50% condensation temperature T₅₀ of an element is its working volatility scale: when T₅₀ is plotted against the Earth/CI ratio, the data form a clean trend — the lower an element's T₅₀, the more depleted it is in the bulk silicate Earth.

concepts.title: Earth's Volatile Depletion and Core Formation
concepts.contentHtml:
Comparing the bulk silicate Earth (BSE) to CI chondrite reveals two superimposed signatures. First, volatile depletion: elements with T₅₀ < ~1300 K are systematically below CI, with the depletion deepening as T₅₀ falls. K (T₅₀ ≈ 1006 K) is depleted by about a factor of seven; Pb is depleted by ~30 ×.

Second, siderophile depletion: elements that prefer metal over silicate (Ni, Co, Mo, W, the platinum-group elements) are stripped out of the silicate Earth and sequestered in the core. Their abundances in BSE are far lower than expected from volatility alone. The pattern fits a single high-pressure equilibrium between molten silicate and a Fe-Ni-S metallic liquid in a deep magma ocean at roughly 40–60 GPa and 3500 K.

The chemical balance — refractory lithophile elements at near-CI levels, moderately volatile elements depleted, siderophiles in the core — is the fingerprint of how Earth was assembled from chondritic precursors and then differentiated within ~30–100 Myr of CAI formation.

title: Goldschmidt Classification and Element Behaviour
description: Lithophile, siderophile, chalcophile, atmophile — and what 'compatible' means

concepts.title: The Four Goldschmidt Affinities
concepts.contentHtml:
Victor Goldschmidt, working in 1920s Oslo on the products of the Norwegian smelting industry, noticed that elements distribute themselves predictably between coexisting metallic, sulfidic, silicate, and gaseous phases. He proposed four affinities. Lithophile elements prefer silicate liquids and oxides; their bonding is largely ionic with O²⁻ (Si, Al, Mg, Ca, K, Na, Ti, the REE, U, Th). Siderophile elements prefer metallic Fe (Ni, Co, Mo, W, Re, Ir, Pt, Au). Chalcophile elements prefer sulfide melts (Cu, Zn, Pb, Ag, Cd, Hg, As). Atmophile elements stay in the gas phase (H, N, noble gases, often C).

The classification is empirical but tracks deeper physics: ionisation energies, electronegativities, and the Pearson hard/soft acid–base character. Hard cations (Ca²⁺, Al³⁺) bond ionically with the hard base O²⁻; soft cations (Pb²⁺, Hg²⁺) prefer the softer S²⁻. Goldschmidt's affinities still organise modern partitioning data with surprising fidelity.

concepts.title: Compatible vs Incompatible: The Igneous Definition
concepts.contentHtml:
In an igneous context, an element is compatible if it prefers the crystalline solid over the silicate melt during partial melting or fractional crystallisation. Incompatible elements prefer the melt. The discriminator is the partition coefficient:

Kd > 1 means compatible (Ni and Cr enter olivine and spinel; Eu²⁺ enters plagioclase); Kd < 1 means incompatible (Rb, K, U, Th, the light REE, large-ion lithophiles).

The same element can flip between categories depending on the mineral assemblage and the redox state. Eu is incompatible in most minerals as Eu³⁺, but at low fO₂ it is partly Eu²⁺, which substitutes neatly for Ca²⁺ in plagioclase — the famous Eu anomaly. Vanadium, Cr and Fe similarly switch behaviour with redox. Compatibility is not a property of an element in isolation; it is a property of an element in a particular mineral, melt, P, T, and fO₂.

concepts.title: Charge, Radius, and the Onuma Diagram
concepts.contentHtml:
For a given crystal lattice site, the partition coefficient is approximately a parabolic function of the cation radius, peaking at the radius that best matches the site. This is captured by the lattice strain model of Blundy and Wood (1994):

Di = D₀ · exp(−4πE·NA·[r₀/2·(rᵢ − r₀)² + ⅓·(rᵢ − r₀)³] / RT), where r₀ is the optimal radius, E is the site Young's modulus, and D₀ is the partition coefficient for the perfect-fit cation.

Plotting log Kd against ionic radius for cations of a given charge gives a parabola — an Onuma diagram — for each crystal site. The diagram explains why divalent cations of intermediate radius (Ca²⁺, Sr²⁺) sit near the peak in plagioclase and why the heavy REE (small) and light REE (large) are progressively excluded. Charge mismatch costs more energy than size mismatch, so cations also prefer their native valence; a 3+ cation must be paired with a 1+ vacancy or coupled substitution to enter a 2+ site.
mathExpressions: D_i = D_0 \exp\!\left(-\frac{4\pi E N_A}{RT}\left[\tfrac{r_0}{2}(r_i - r_0)^2 + \tfrac{1}{3}(r_i - r_0)^3\right]\right)

title: Trace Elements, REE Patterns, and the Eu Anomaly
description: From Henry's law to chondrite-normalised diagrams

concepts.title: Henry's Law and Bulk Partition Coefficients
concepts.contentHtml:
Trace elements occupy lattice sites in mineral crystals at concentrations low enough (< ~0.1 wt%) that they don't interact with each other. In this dilute limit they obey Henry's law: the activity of the trace element in a phase is linearly proportional to its concentration. The proportionality constant is the partition coefficient Kd.

For a polymineralic source (the upper mantle is roughly 60% olivine, 25% orthopyroxene, 10% clinopyroxene, 5% garnet or spinel), each mineral has its own Kd. The composite bulk partition coefficient is the modal-weighted sum:

Dbulk = Σ Xj · Kdj, where Xj is the mass fraction of mineral j in the source.

Dbulk is the master parameter for melting models — it sets how aggressively a trace element is extracted into the melt and therefore how strongly its abundance grows in residual mantle versus enriched melt.

concepts.title: Equilibrium vs Fractional Melting
concepts.contentHtml:
Two end-member melting laws bracket reality. Batch (equilibrium) melting assumes the melt stays in chemical equilibrium with the residue until it is extracted in a single batch:

CL/C0 = 1 / [D + F(1 − D)],

where F is melt fraction. Fractional melting assumes each infinitesimal melt increment leaves immediately, so the residue progressively depletes:

CL/C0 = (1/D) · (1 − F)(1/D − 1).

The two diverge dramatically for highly incompatible elements (D ≪ 1). At F = 0.05 with D = 0.001, batch melting concentrates the element ~20 ×, fractional melting concentrates the very first drop ~1000 ×. Real melting under mid-ocean ridges sits between the two, modelled as continuous (dynamic) melting — a porosity-controlled compromise. The takeaway: incompatible elements are exquisitely sensitive to the mechanism, not just the amount, of melting.

concepts.title: REE Patterns and the Eu Anomaly
concepts.contentHtml:
The rare earth elements (La through Lu, plus Y) form a coherent +3 series whose ionic radius decreases smoothly across the lanthanide contraction. Plotting their concentrations divided by CI chondrite values on a log scale against atomic number gives a smooth curve — the chondrite-normalised REE pattern — that fingerprints petrogenetic history.

Light-REE-enriched, heavy-REE-depleted patterns indicate small-degree melting in the presence of garnet (which holds HREE back). Flat patterns indicate large-degree melting or a primitive source. Eu is the diagnostic outlier: under reducing conditions it becomes Eu²⁺, which substitutes for Ca²⁺ in plagioclase. Plagioclase fractionation drives a negative Eu anomaly in the residual melt; plagioclase accumulation gives a positive Eu anomaly.

The anomaly is quantified as Eu/Eu* = EuN / √(SmN · GdN). Continental crust averages Eu/Eu* ≈ 0.65 (negative) — a fingerprint of plagioclase-fractionating processes deep in its history. Lunar highland anorthosites show strongly positive Eu anomalies, consistent with their plagioclase-cumulate origin.

title: Radiogenic Isotope Systems
description: K-Ar, Rb-Sr, Sm-Nd, U-Pb, Lu-Hf, Re-Os: which clock for which mineral

concepts.title: The Decay Equation and the Isochron
concepts.contentHtml:
Radioactive decay is first-order: the number of parent atoms N(t) = N₀ e−λt, with decay constant λ and half-life t½ = ln 2 / λ. The daughter grows in by D(t) = D₀ + N₀(1 − e−λt) = D₀ + N(t)·(eλt − 1), where N(t) is the present-day parent count.

To use this as a clock, pick a stable reference isotope of the daughter (e.g. ⁸⁶Sr for the Rb-Sr system) and divide through. For a suite of cogenetic minerals that crystallised at the same t with the same initial daughter ratio:

(⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr)now = (⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr)init + (⁸⁷Rb/⁸⁶Sr)now·(eλt − 1).

This is a straight line — the isochron — when plotted as (⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr) vs (⁸⁷Rb/⁸⁶Sr). The slope gives the age, the intercept gives the initial daughter ratio. Isochrons are robust because they need no assumption about the initial daughter abundance.

concepts.title: The Workhorse Decay Constants
concepts.contentHtml:
Each system has its own λ, half-life, suitable mineral hosts, and closure temperature. The major systems geochronologists rely on:

K-Ar / ⁴⁰Ar-³⁹Ar: λtotal(⁴⁰K) = 5.543 × 10⁻¹⁰ yr⁻¹, t½ ≈ 1.25 Ga. Branching decay to ⁴⁰Ar (10.7%) and ⁴⁰Ca (89.3%). Hosts: micas, K-feldspar, hornblende. Closure 200–550 °C.

Rb-Sr: λ(⁸⁷Rb) = 1.397 × 10⁻¹¹ yr⁻¹, t½ ≈ 49.6 Ga. Hosts: micas, K-feldspar, whole rock. Mobile in fluids, easily reset.

Sm-Nd: λ(¹⁴⁷Sm) = 6.54 × 10⁻¹² yr⁻¹, t½ ≈ 106 Ga. Hosts: garnet, clinopyroxene, whole rock. Refractory, fluid-resistant — excellent for ancient mafic rocks.

U-Pb: dual decay of ²³⁸U (λ = 1.5513 × 10⁻¹⁰ yr⁻¹) and ²³⁵U (λ = 9.8485 × 10⁻¹⁰ yr⁻¹). Host: zircon. The most precise system available.

Lu-Hf: λ(¹⁷⁶Lu) = 1.867 × 10⁻¹¹ yr⁻¹. Hosts: garnet, zircon. Re-Os: λ(¹⁸⁷Re) = 1.666 × 10⁻¹¹ yr⁻¹. Hosts: molybdenite, sulfides — the only practical system for dating ore mineralisation directly.

concepts.title: Closure Temperature and What a Date Means
concepts.contentHtml:
Diffusion of the daughter through the mineral lattice is finite at high temperature. Above some closure temperature Tc, the daughter escapes as fast as it is produced and the clock is open; below Tc, diffusion is negligible and the clock starts. Tc depends on mineral, grain size, and cooling rate, given by Dodson (1973):

Tc = E / [R · ln(A·R·Tc²·D₀ / (E·a²·dT/dt))], solved iteratively.

Approximate closure temperatures: zircon U-Pb > 900 °C, monazite U-Pb ~ 700 °C, garnet Sm-Nd ~ 600 °C, hornblende ⁴⁰Ar/³⁹Ar ~ 530 °C, muscovite Ar-Ar ~ 400 °C, biotite Ar-Ar ~ 320 °C, K-feldspar Ar-Ar 150–300 °C, apatite (U-Th)/He ~ 70 °C.

Therefore a single rock can carry several different "ages," each marking the moment a particular mineral cooled through its closure temperature. The hierarchy of Tc is the basis of thermochronology, which reconstructs cooling and exhumation histories from a coordinated suite of dates on different minerals.

title: U-Pb Geochronology and the Concordia
description: Why zircon rules deep time — and how to read its imperfections

concepts.title: The Two Independent U-Pb Clocks
concepts.contentHtml:
Uranium has two long-lived isotopes, ²³⁸U and ²³⁵U, each decaying through a long chain to a different stable Pb isotope (²⁰⁶Pb and ²⁰⁷Pb respectively). Because both clocks tick in the same crystal but at different rates, U-Pb gives a built-in cross-check.

The two daughter/parent ratios at time t are:

(²⁰⁶Pb*/²³⁸U) = eλ₂₃₈ t − 1 and (²⁰⁷Pb*/²³⁵U) = eλ₂₃₅ t − 1.

The locus of (²⁰⁷Pb*/²³⁵U, ²⁰⁶Pb*/²³⁸U) traced out as t varies from 0 to 4.6 Ga is the Wetherill concordia — a curved line in this diagram. A closed-system mineral falls on the curve. Discordant data fall off it. The third independent ratio (²⁰⁷Pb*/²⁰⁶Pb*) self-corrects for U content and gives the most precise age for ancient samples — the famous Pb-Pb age.

concepts.title: Discordia, Pb-Loss, and Inheritance
concepts.contentHtml:
Real zircon grains are rarely perfectly concordant. Pb-loss from radiation-damaged (metamict) domains, inheritance of older cores, or partial recrystallisation during metamorphism all pull data points off the concordia. Plotted as ²⁰⁶Pb/²³⁸U vs ²⁰⁷Pb/²³⁵U, those points typically scatter along a chord — a discordia line.

The discordia intersects the concordia at two ages: the upper intercept usually records the original crystallisation age, and the lower intercept records a younger event (Pb-loss episode, metamorphism, modern weathering at 0 Ma). The Vredefort impact structure in South Africa famously gives a discordia upper intercept of ~3.07 Ga (granitic basement) with a lower intercept of ~2.02 Ga, recording the impact event itself.

Modern chemical abrasion ID-TIMS pre-treatment dissolves metamict domains before analysis, leaving only crystalline cores; this routinely recovers concordant ages with 0.05% precision (~1 Myr at 2 Ga). The Jack Hills detrital zircons reach 4.40 Ga with this method — the oldest known terrestrial material.

concepts.title: ID-TIMS vs LA-ICP-MS, and Common-Pb
concepts.contentHtml:
Two analytical methods dominate U-Pb today, with very different trade-offs.

ID-TIMS (isotope-dilution thermal ionisation mass spectrometry) dissolves a single zircon (often a fragment), spikes it with a calibrated ²⁰²Pb-²⁰⁵Pb-²³³U-²³⁵U tracer (the EARTHTIME ET2535 spike), and measures isotope ratios on a multicollector mass spectrometer. Precisions of 0.05–0.1% are routine. Slow (days per grain), expensive, but the gold standard.

LA-ICP-MS ablates a 20–50 µm laser pit, pipes the aerosol into a plasma source mass spectrometer, and gets a date in 30 seconds. Precisions of 1–2%. Cheap, fast, spatially resolved — perfect for detrital surveys and zoned grains, but not for high-precision tie-points.

Both methods must correct for common Pb — Pb that was incorporated when the mineral grew rather than produced by U decay. Zircons exclude Pb during growth (Pb²⁺ doesn't fit the Zr⁴⁺ site), so common Pb is usually small and can be subtracted using the non-radiogenic ²⁰⁴Pb monitor: ²⁰⁶Pb*/²³⁸U = (²⁰⁶Pb/²³⁸U)meas − (²⁰⁶Pb/²⁰⁴Pb)cm · (²⁰⁴Pb/²³⁸U)meas.

title: Stable Isotopes and Mass-Dependent Fractionation
description: δ-notation, equilibrium and kinetic effects, paleothermometry

concepts.title: δ-Notation and the Reference Standards
concepts.contentHtml:
Mass differences between isotopes of the same element produce small but measurable fractionations during physical, chemical, and biological processes. Because absolute ratios are hard to measure precisely but ratio differences are easy, results are reported in delta notation relative to an international standard:

δiX = [(Rsample / Rstd) − 1] × 1000 ‰, where R = heavy/light isotope ratio.

Standards are anchored physical materials. VSMOW (Vienna Standard Mean Ocean Water) for δ¹⁸O and δD of waters. VPDB (Vienna Pee Dee Belemnite) for δ¹³C of carbonates and δ¹⁸O of carbonates. VCDT (Vienna Canyon Diablo Troilite) for δ³⁴S. AIR for δ¹⁵N. A modern continuous-flow IRMS measures these to ±0.1‰ routinely; high-precision dual-inlet to ±0.01‰.

By convention, δ values are positive when the sample is enriched in the heavy isotope relative to the standard. Ocean water sits at δ¹⁸O = 0‰ (it defines the standard); polar ice can reach −55‰; modern marine carbonate sits near 0‰ on VPDB.

concepts.title: Equilibrium and Kinetic Fractionation
concepts.contentHtml:
Two regimes generate isotope fractionation. Equilibrium fractionation arises because heavier isotopes form slightly stronger bonds (lower vibrational zero-point energy). Between two phases A and B at temperature T, the equilibrium fractionation factor αA-B = RA/RB obeys 1000 ln α ≈ A/T² + B/T + C, with the temperature dependence diminishing at high T. The classic carbonate–water oxygen isotope thermometer of Kim and O'Neil (1997):

1000 ln αcc-w = 18.03(10³/T) − 32.42 (T in K).

This means a 1 °C cooling raises δ¹⁸O of precipitated calcite by ~0.23‰. Foraminifera calcified in equilibrium with seawater therefore record paleotemperatures.

Kinetic fractionation is a one-way process: lighter isotopes diffuse and react slightly faster. Photosynthesis discriminates against ¹³C (Rubisco prefers ¹²CO₂), giving plant tissue δ¹³C of −25 to −35‰ for C3 plants and −10 to −15‰ for C4 plants. Bacterial sulfate reduction can fractionate ³⁴S by 30–60‰.

concepts.title: Paleothermometry, the Carbon Cycle, and δ¹⁵N / δ³⁴S
concepts.contentHtml:
The classic application is oxygen-isotope paleothermometry: foraminiferal CaCO₃ records δ¹⁸O depending on growth temperature and seawater δ¹⁸O. The Cenozoic δ¹⁸O curve from benthic foraminifera (Zachos et al. 2001) traces 65 Myr of climate cooling, glacial onsets, and Pleistocene cycles; ice volume and temperature both contribute, and disentangling them is the central problem of paleoceanography.

The carbon cycle imprints δ¹³C across reservoirs: marine carbonate ≈ 0‰, atmospheric CO₂ ≈ −8.5‰ today (preindustrial −6.5‰), C3 plants ≈ −27‰, methane from methanogenesis can reach −60‰. Burial of organic carbon withdraws ¹²C from the ocean, raising marine δ¹³C; the great Lomagundi-Jatuli excursion at 2.2–2.0 Ga (δ¹³C ≈ +10‰ for hundreds of Myr) records a vast organic-carbon burial event tied to early atmospheric oxygenation.

δ¹⁵N traces nitrogen cycling: trophic-level enrichment of ~3‰ per step makes it a forensic tool. δ³⁴S tracks sulfide oxidation, sulfate reduction, and the long-term redox state of the ocean. Stable isotopes are the most flexible tracers in geochemistry — applicable from individual cells to the deep mantle.

title: Cosmogenic and Short-Lived Isotopes
description: ¹⁴C, ¹⁰Be, ²⁶Al, and U-series disequilibria

concepts.title: Radiocarbon Dating and the Atmosphere
concepts.contentHtml:
¹⁴C is produced continuously in the upper atmosphere when secondary cosmic-ray neutrons react with ¹⁴N: ¹⁴N(n,p)¹⁴C. The resulting ¹⁴C oxidises to ¹⁴CO₂, mixes through the atmosphere and ocean, and is incorporated into living tissue at the atmospheric ratio (modern pre-bomb ≈ 1.2 × 10⁻¹² ¹⁴C/¹²C). When an organism dies, exchange ceases and ¹⁴C decays with t½ = 5730 years (the "Cambridge half-life"; Libby's original 5568 yr is still used by convention for raw ages, then calibrated).

Modern accelerator mass spectrometry counts ¹⁴C atoms directly rather than detecting decays, giving useful precisions to ~50,000 years (about 9 half-lives, when sample ¹⁴C drops to atmospheric blank levels). Calibration against tree-ring sequences (IntCal20) and Hulu Cave speleothems converts radiocarbon years to calendar years, accommodating past variations in atmospheric ¹⁴C from solar activity, geomagnetic field changes, and the suess effect of fossil-fuel burning.

concepts.title: Cosmogenic Surface-Exposure Dating
concepts.contentHtml:
Cosmic-ray spallation of target nuclei in surface rocks produces measurable amounts of ¹⁰Be, ²⁶Al, ³⁶Cl, ³He, and ²¹Ne in situ. The production rate at sea level, high latitude is ~4.0 ¹⁰Be atoms per gram of quartz per year; it scales exponentially with altitude (factor of ~5 at 4000 m) and with geomagnetic latitude.

For a flat surface continuously exposed for time t with no erosion, the buildup is N(t) = (P/λ)·(1 − e−λt). For ¹⁰Be (t½ = 1.387 Ma) over a few tens of kyr, λt ≪ 1 and N ≈ P·t. With erosion at rate ε, steady-state gives Nss ≈ P/(λ + ε/Λ), where Λ ≈ 160 g cm⁻² is the cosmic-ray attenuation length. ¹⁰Be in quartz dates moraines, glacial pavements, and fluvial terraces from ~10² to 10⁶ years. Pairing ¹⁰Be with ²⁶Al (different half-lives) deconvolves exposure age from burial age — the basis of ²⁶Al/¹⁰Be burial dating used to date hominin-bearing cave sediments.

concepts.title: U-Series Disequilibria and Magma Timescales
concepts.contentHtml:
The decay chain ²³⁸U → ²³⁴U → ²³⁰Th → ²²⁶Ra → ²²²Rn → ²¹⁰Pb → ²⁰⁶Pb passes through nuclides with half-lives ranging from 245 ka (²³⁴U) to 5.5 days (²²²Rn). In a closed system undisturbed for ~5 half-lives of the longest-lived intermediate, all members reach secular equilibrium: their activities (λN) are equal.

Any geochemical process that fractionates parent from daughter (partial melting, weathering, biogenic uptake) creates disequilibrium that decays back over the timescale of the relevant half-life. Th is more incompatible than U during partial melting, so young MORB and OIB show (²³⁰Th/²³⁸U) > 1 — direct evidence that melting was recent (≪ 350 ka) and the magma transit time was short.

²³⁰Th-²³⁴U dating of speleothems (used in Hulu Cave for the IntCal calibration) and corals reaches back to ~600 ka with ~0.1% precision. ²¹⁰Pb (t½ = 22.3 yr) dates the most recent century of lake and estuary sediments — the geochemistry of the Anthropocene.

title: Mantle Geochemistry and Endmembers
description: MORB, OIB, and the four flavours of mantle: DMM, EM1, EM2, HIMU

concepts.title: Depleted vs Enriched Mantle: MORB and OIB
concepts.contentHtml:
Two volcanic suites carry most of the chemical information about the mantle. Mid-ocean-ridge basalts (MORB) erupt continuously along ~65,000 km of spreading ridges and sample the upper mantle that has lost incompatible elements to the continental crust. They have low ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr (~0.7025), high ¹⁴³Nd/¹⁴⁴Nd (εNd ~ +9 to +12), low ²⁰⁶Pb/²⁰⁴Pb (~17.5–18.5), low LREE/HREE — the signature of a long-term depleted mantle.

Ocean-island basalts (OIB) from hotspots (Hawaii, Iceland, Réunion) carry more variable, generally enriched signatures: higher ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr, lower εNd, often high ²⁰⁶Pb/²⁰⁴Pb, and elevated incompatible-element abundances. Helium-3/Helium-4 ratios in OIB are systematically higher than MORB, suggesting a deep, less-degassed source.

The picture: the upper mantle has been depleted by ~3 Ga of continental-crust extraction; deeper mantle reservoirs have been less stirred and preserve more primitive or recycled signatures, sampled when plumes rise through the depleted upper mantle and erupt at hotspots.

concepts.title: The Mantle Endmembers: DMM, EM1, EM2, HIMU
concepts.contentHtml:
Plotting OIB suites on Sr-Nd-Pb-Hf isotope diagrams reveals an array that is bounded by four endmembers, identified by Zindler and Hart (1986).

DMM (depleted MORB mantle): low ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr, high εNd, low ²⁰⁶Pb/²⁰⁴Pb. The well-mixed upper-mantle reservoir.

EM1 (enriched mantle 1): moderately high ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr, low εNd, low ²⁰⁶Pb/²⁰⁴Pb. Best example: Pitcairn, Walvis Ridge. Often interpreted as recycled lower continental crust or pelagic sediment.

EM2 (enriched mantle 2): the highest ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr (up to 0.722 at Samoa), moderate ²⁰⁶Pb/²⁰⁴Pb. Consistent with subducted upper-continental-crust sediment.

HIMU (high-µ, where µ ≡ ²³⁸U/²⁰⁴Pb): exceptionally high ²⁰⁶Pb/²⁰⁴Pb (> 21), moderate Sr and Nd. Best examples: St. Helena, Cook-Austral. Likely represents recycled altered oceanic crust ~1.5–2.5 Ga old, where U was added by hydrothermal alteration and Pb has grown ever since.

Real OIB compositions are mixtures of these endmembers plus DMM, sketching a four-component petrologic map of the deep Earth.

concepts.title: CHUR, the Bulk Earth Reference, and Mantle Mixing
concepts.contentHtml:
To track relative enrichment we need a baseline. CHUR (chondritic uniform reservoir) is defined as a hypothetical reservoir with the present-day Sm/Nd and Lu/Hf ratios of average chondrites. Bulk Earth is assumed to track CHUR for refractory lithophile ratios. The deviation of a sample from CHUR is reported as εNd or εHf in parts per 10,000:

εNd = [(¹⁴³Nd/¹⁴⁴Nd)sample / (¹⁴³Nd/¹⁴⁴Nd)CHUR − 1] × 10⁴.

Recent stable-isotope work on ¹⁴²Nd / ¹⁴⁴Nd suggests Earth may have a slight ~+0.18 ε deviation from CHUR, perhaps due to early differentiation events, but to first approximation the chondritic reference holds.

The mantle is a stirred, partly homogenised system: continental extraction depletes the upper part; subduction returns altered oceanic crust and sediments that re-enrich it. Two-reservoir models with mass-balance (e.g. Allègre and Lewin, 1995) and tomographic imaging of slab graveyards near the core-mantle boundary now agree the convective mixing time of the whole mantle is on the order of 1–2 Ga — long enough to preserve the geochemical heterogeneity we see in OIB but short enough to produce a broadly homogeneous upper-mantle MORB source.

title: Hadean Earth, the Moon, and W Isotopes
description: Crust-mantle differentiation, the giant impact, and ¹⁸²Hf-¹⁸²W chronometry

concepts.title: The Hadean and the Jack Hills Zircons
concepts.contentHtml:
The Hadean eon (4.567–4.0 Ga) has almost no rock record because Earth's surface has been continuously recycled. The exception: detrital zircons in the Jack Hills metaconglomerate of Western Australia, eroded from now-vanished sources and incorporated into a ~3.0 Ga sediment. Individual zircons reach U-Pb ages of 4.40 Ga (Wilde et al. 2001).

Their oxygen isotopes (δ¹⁸O up to +7.5‰) imply formation from magmas that interacted with low-temperature surface water, suggesting that liquid water existed on Earth's surface within ~150 Myr of accretion. Their Lu-Hf systematics (εHf as low as −5 at 4.4 Ga) require derivation from older, evolved crust — meaning that some form of granitic protocrust existed in the deep Hadean. The picture has shifted from a uniformly molten "Hadean hellscape" to a planet that, surprisingly quickly, had oceans and continents in some form.

concepts.title: ¹⁸²Hf-¹⁸²W: Dating Core Formation
concepts.contentHtml:
The extinct nuclide ¹⁸²Hf decays to ¹⁸²W with t½ = 8.9 Myr — far too short-lived to survive today, but active during the first ~50 Myr of the solar system. Hf is lithophile (stays in the silicate mantle); W is moderately siderophile (goes to the core). If core formation happens before ¹⁸²Hf has fully decayed, the silicate mantle inherits a Hf/W ratio higher than chondritic and grows excess ¹⁸²W; the metallic core is locked in with chondritic ¹⁸²W/¹⁸⁴W.

The bulk silicate Earth's ε¹⁸²W ≈ +1.9 (relative to chondrites) implies core formation was largely complete within ~30–60 Myr of CAI formation. Lunar samples show ε¹⁸²W within error of Earth's mantle, anchoring the moon-formation time to a similar window. The Hf-W system is the cleanest chronometer of metal-silicate differentiation we have — short half-life, big chemical fractionation, no surface contamination.

concepts.title: The Moon-Forming Impact and the Late Veneer
concepts.contentHtml:
The leading model for lunar origin is the giant impact of a Mars-sized body ("Theia") with proto-Earth at ~60 Myr after CAI. Predicted geochemical consequences: the Moon should be silicate-rich (no large iron core); volatile-depleted (high temperatures during impact); and isotopically similar to Earth in O, Ti, Cr, K, and W within ~5 ppm. Apollo samples confirm all these.

The very tight similarity in Δ¹⁷O (within 5 ppm of Earth's mantle) is the puzzle: it suggests Earth and Theia formed in the same isotopic neighbourhood, or that the post-impact magma equilibrated more thoroughly than simple impact dynamics predict.

After core formation, the silicate Earth still has ~0.05% chondritic abundances of highly siderophile elements (Os, Ir, Pt, Pd) — too high if all metal had partitioned to the core. The favoured explanation is a late veneer: ~0.5% of Earth's mass added as chondritic material after core formation, replenishing siderophile elements in the upper mantle. This late veneer is also a candidate source of much of Earth's water and atmophile inventory.

title: Modern Frontiers and Environmental Forensics
description: Non-traditional stable isotopes, clumped isotopes, and triple-oxygen MIF

concepts.title: Non-Traditional Stable Isotopes (Mg, Fe, Cu, Zn, Mo)
concepts.contentHtml:
For decades, only H, C, N, O, S were measurable to sub-permil precision. Multi-collector ICP-MS (MC-ICP-MS) since the late 1990s has opened the rest of the periodic table to high-precision stable-isotope work. δ²⁶Mg, δ⁵⁶Fe, δ⁶⁵Cu, δ⁶⁶Zn, δ⁹⁵Mo, δ⁵³Cr, δ⁹⁸Mo, and many more are now routinely measured to ±0.05‰.

Each tracks specific processes. δ⁵⁶Fe distinguishes biotic Fe(II)/Fe(III) cycling from abiotic — banded iron formations show lighter δ⁵⁶Fe than seawater, fingerprinting microbial Fe oxidation in the Archean ocean. δ⁹⁸Mo in euxinic sediments approaches seawater values when bottom waters are sulfidic, providing a global ocean redox proxy through deep time.

The CI-chondrite normalised isotopic composition of bulk Earth is now constrained for these elements, and small (~50 ppm) anomalies in early-solar-system materials reveal nucleosynthetic heterogeneity inherited from different stellar sources of pre-solar dust.

concepts.title: Clumped Isotopes (Δ47) and Triple-Oxygen MIF
concepts.contentHtml:
Clumped isotope thermometry measures the abundance of doubly-substituted isotopologues — for carbonates, the ¹³C¹⁸O¹⁶O₂²⁻ species (mass 47). At thermodynamic equilibrium, heavy isotopes "clump" preferentially at low temperatures. The Δ47 value (excess of mass-47 isotopologues over the random distribution) thus provides a temperature-only thermometer that does not require knowledge of seawater δ¹⁸O:

Δ47 ≈ 0.0449 × 10⁶/T² + offset (T in K), giving useful precisions of ±2 °C with hours of measurement. Clumped isotopes have re-evaluated dinosaur body temperatures, paleosol temperatures across the Cenozoic, and the formation conditions of carbonate cements.

Triple-oxygen mass-independent fractionation (MIF) breaks the mass-dependent law that δ¹⁷O ≈ 0.52·δ¹⁸O. Atmospheric ozone formation produces O₃ with anomalous Δ¹⁷O (= δ¹⁷O − 0.52·δ¹⁸O) of up to +30‰. This signal is transferred to atmospheric sulfate and nitrate. Δ¹⁷O in Archean sulfides (Farquhar et al. 2000) shows large MIF before 2.45 Ga and none after — direct geochemical evidence for the rise of atmospheric O₂ shielding UV photochemistry, the Great Oxidation Event.

concepts.title: Environmental Geochemistry: Source Tracing
concepts.contentHtml:
Stable and radiogenic isotopes have become the forensic tool of environmental science. Lead isotopes (²⁰⁶Pb/²⁰⁷Pb) fingerprint the source of Pb contamination in soils, blood, and ice cores: Australian Pb (Broken Hill ore, ²⁰⁶Pb/²⁰⁷Pb ≈ 1.04) used in leaded petrol leaves a different signature from US Mississippi-Valley Pb (~1.20). Greenland ice records the rise and fall of leaded petrol globally between 1923 and 2000.

Arsenic in Bangladesh groundwater — affecting tens of millions through chronic As poisoning from shallow tube wells — is sourced from natural As-bearing pyrite in deltaic aquifer sediments, mobilised by reductive dissolution of Fe-oxyhydroxides. δ³⁴S, δ¹⁵N, and Fe isotopes together resolve the redox processes driving the release.

Nitrate δ¹⁵N and δ¹⁸O distinguish synthetic-fertiliser nitrate (low δ¹⁵N, low δ¹⁸O) from manure/septic nitrate (high δ¹⁵N) from atmospheric deposition (very high δ¹⁸O). Source apportionment in agricultural watersheds now routinely uses dual-isotope plots. Geochemistry has become a tool of environmental policy — the same ratios that track 4-billion-year-old planet formation also track this morning's pollution plume.
